extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics instructors, new instructors, teaching assistants, and instructor trainers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and recommended activities for mathematics instructors on proctoring/returning exams, handling grade disputes and cheating, and incorporating graphing calculators/Computer Algebra Systems (CAS) into teaching and instructor training meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor repeated/excessive exits during exams
rubrics_metrics.description: If a student is gone for a long time, or asks to leave the room repeatedly, then it is probably time to get suspicious, and perhaps time to insist on an escort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat frequent or long absences during an exam as a security concern; consider insisting that the student be escorted to prevent cheating or collusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make returned exams informative but manage class disruption
rubrics_metrics.description: When returning papers to students, it is important for students to understand what mistakes they made. Many students feel that it is important to understand why they weren’t given more points on the exam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh benefits of walking through an exam against the likelihood of interruptions and protests (e.g., 'But that’s exactly what I wrote!'); a whole class period devoted to going over an exam can be futile and disruptive—consider alternatives or restrict in-class review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of returning graded exams
rubrics_metrics.description: If you decide to return graded exams in class, you may find it least disruptive to return the exams at the end of the class period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Returning exams at the end of class reduces class-time disruption. If posting summary information, consider doing so at the beginning of the first class after the exam, but be mindful of morale effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posting class statistics (means/medians) when returning exams
rubrics_metrics.description: Some instructors post information (such as means or medians) on the board at the beginning of class, to indicate how well the class did as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posting the class average can boost morale if scores are good, but can raise serious questions and anxiety if not. Consider privacy, context, and consequences before posting; announce any policies beforehand to prevent tampering.

rubrics_metrics.name: "If the exam leaves the room, I can't make any changes to the score" policy
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to prevent students from trying to alter their answers, some instructors announce an 'If the exam leaves the room, I can’t make any changes to the score,' policy before returning papers to students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this policy to deter post-return alterations; make the policy explicit before returning exams. Encourage students who want detailed review to meet privately so the instructor retains a pre-return copy or control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer private pickup/review during office hours
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative approach is to have students come to office hours, or make short appointments, to pick up their exams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: (a) handle grade complaints privately, (b) work through poorly answered parts individually, (c) put each student's score into context and advise on options, (d) prevents opportunity to modify exams (if combined with the 'exam leaves the room' policy). Note: meeting individually may be time-consuming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reveal specific individuals' performances
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not discuss with students how specific individuals performed on the exam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer requests for others' scores with descriptive statistics (mean/median) or anonymized position (e.g., first, second) only if comfortable; never reveal names—this violates privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not name students when discussing grades with colleagues
rubrics_metrics.description: If you discuss grades with other instructors, please do not name names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect student privacy when consulting colleagues about grading or student performance; use anonymized data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid discussing perceived student ability publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not discuss your perception of a student’s ability in front of other students, whether from your own class or from another class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep evaluative or diagnostic comments about a student's ability private to avoid embarrassment and preserve trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not re-grade exams in front of students
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not re-grade exams in front of students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-grading publicly can create perceptions of unfairness or open debate; handle regrade processes privately and consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid in-class debates about grading fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not get into debates over grading policies, or the fairness of exam questions. If students press, then point out that everyone took the same exam, and the same grading scheme was applied to everyone’s paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defer detailed disputes to private meetings; remind students of uniform application of grading scheme to maintain consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require written statements for regrade requests
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have students who insist on having their exam re-graded, it is often very helpful to ask the students to write a statement explaining why they deserve more credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate regrade requests based on the written statement; students who are merely 'grubbing' for points will typically fail to point to specific grading errors. Avoid re-grading to a different standard for individual students to preserve fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent post-return cheating without mass copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying every single exam is wasteful and unnecessary. A policy along the lines of, 'If the exam leaves the room, I can’t make any changes to the score,' will achieve the same result in almost all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer policies and controlled pickup procedures over copying every exam. Encourage detailed review via supervised or private meetings to reduce alteration risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote honesty as a group norm to reduce cheating
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing a class atmosphere that has 'honesty as a group norm' and building instructor-student relationships removes anonymity that may lead students to believe they will not get caught cheating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate relationships and norms that value honesty; treat disciplinary committees as potentially constructive rather than purely punitive to help students long-term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate technology thoughtfully (avoid shortcuts)
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not advocate the use of technology as a way for students to 'short-cut' their learning process by learning some calculator or computer commands by rote. The use of graphing calculators and CAS in elementary mathematics courses can be a great boost to student learning, but for this to be so the technology must be thoughtfully and carefully incorporated into the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure technology supports conceptual understanding rather than rote command memorization. Plan activities so technology enables higher-order tasks instead of replacing foundational skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technology to shift emphasis to Polya steps 1,2,4
rubrics_metrics.description: With access to appropriate technology, students can spend more time involved with steps 1 (understand the problem), 2 (devise a plan), and 4 (look back), while leaving much of step 3 (carry out the plan) to a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that leverage technology for computation while emphasizing problem formulation, strategy, and reflection; do not abandon manual computation entirely where it's pedagogically important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five categories of using technology as a teaching tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The categories of use summarized are: Discovery—learning by discovery; Algorithms—using the programming capabilities to expedite calculation algorithms that are tedious by hand; Visualization—visualizing mathematical notions; Solving Problems—allowing the student to solve problems that without the use of technology would be beyond their current mathematical tools; Connecting Multiple Representations—connecting graphical, numerical, and algebraic approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning activities, classify them into these categories and choose examples that make the pedagogical role of technology clear (e.g., discovery activities for conjecture formation, algorithms for iteration/approximation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for a 50-minute instructor training meeting on technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Goals: (1) help instructors think about how technology can be used to help achieve course goals; (2) introduce five categories of activities; (3) show specific examples from each category; (4) provide forum to share ideas; (5) discuss how to enhance student learning in upcoming sections; (6) consider potential drawbacks and how to avoid them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the meeting to meet these explicit goals—mix demonstration, hands-on activities, and discussion of pitfalls and solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation checklist for the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare an overhead of the goals; obtain an overhead projecting calculator or computer with projector (or reserve lab); select activities to demonstrate; obtain numerical integration program if needed; practice activities and time them; consider inviting experienced instructors; circulate agenda in advance; ensure participants know to bring calculators or that meeting is in a lab; make copies of materials and confirm attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete logistics and rehearsal in advance so demonstrations run smoothly; time each activity to fit the 50-minute session and prioritize accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda and time-management for the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested agenda: discussion of course goals and how tech achieves them; outline five categories with demonstrated examples; forum for instructors to share ideas; discussion of potential drawbacks. Suggested timing: :01–:05 intro; :05–:10 pass out handout; :10–:30 lead activities; :30–:35 share ideas; :35–:45 discuss drawbacks; :45–:50 wrap-up/questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose activities based on course emphasis and available time; remind instructors that in-class implementation will require more time than a training demo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate misleading graphical displays
rubrics_metrics.description: The graphical displays of graphs (especially those displayed on LCD screens with limited resolution) can be misleading if taken at face value (e.g., global behavior of y = e^x cos x may be misread).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (e.g., misdisplayed asymptotes, under-sampling of sine graphs) to teach students about limitations of plots; encourage analytical checks alongside graphical inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of technical shortcomings of calculators vs CAS
rubrics_metrics.description: Many graphing calculators mismanage asymptotes and gloss over discontinuities; most CAS handle these issues better than hand-held calculators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate specific calculator failures (e.g., y = 1/(x-1) or functions with removable/essential discontinuities) and show how CAS and analytic reasoning can correct misconceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid technology becoming a crutch or causing unlearning
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculators and computers can be a crutch, and cause students to unlearn things that they know (e.g., simple arithmetic) or to overlook obvious simplifications that aid understanding (e.g., simplifications like sin^2 + cos^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which manual skills are essential and design tasks and assessments that preserve those skills while using technology for higher-level tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate calculators as barriers to classroom interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Because each student may have his or her own calculator, the machines can be a physical barrier to interaction; students may interact with their device rather than other students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shared terminals or paired work (e.g., computer lab) to promote collaboration and discussion rather than isolated device use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address assessment questions raised by CAS use
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculators and especially CAS raise tricky assessment issues: instructors must decide which algebraic skills students should still master, which types of problems gain importance with technology, and be aware that the intent of certain problems may be compromised by technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state learning outcomes, design assessment items that test both conceptual understanding and appropriate manual skills, and avoid artificially general problems that undercut technology integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for equity issues with varied calculator models
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculators raise equity issues when different students own different models; problems need to be crafted to avoid advantaging a particular model. This may be reduced if students use CAS on department-provided computers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either standardize allowed devices for assessments or design problems that are device-agnostic; provide lab access when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exam security concerns with networked computers and programmable devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Networked computers may provide students access to prohibited references or communication during exams; programmable calculators can store notes (electronic crib sheets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider exam environment and allowed technology carefully; if technology is used, secure/test exam setups and limit networking or programmable storage where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting materials required
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide copies of 'Technology as a Teaching Tool' handout and 'Learning Activities' handout; working graphing calculator (with overhead projection) or computer with projector running department CAS (or lab); numerical integration program if planning Riemann sums activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble and test all materials in advance; ensure projection and software compatibility for demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity: Discovering the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Use integration capabilities to graph F(x)=∫_0^x f(t) dt and graph F'(x) simultaneously with f(x); if no derivative capability, approximate derivative via difference quotient, and compare F(x) with a known antiderivative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students experiment with several functions and surmise the theorem; alternate approach: use slope-field program and plot integrals with varying lower limits. Example Maple commands provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity: Approximating functions using polynomials (Taylor discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Have students discover tangent-line approximation, then 'guess and check' degree-2 polynomials before introducing Taylor formulas; use plots to find intervals where approximations are indistinguishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage exploratory plotting to build intuition before formal Taylor series; discuss what 'better' means in approximation contexts; follow with degree-4 polynomial experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity: Evaluating integrals numerically (Riemann sums)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use programmable calculators or CAS to run numerical integration algorithms (Riemann sums) to allow many iterations formerly inaccessible by hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide programs in advance or load them on lab machines; use this activity when time permits—it may be skipped if pressed for time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity: Visualizing the derivative via secant lines and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot f(x) and the secant-line expression ((f(a+h)-f(a))/h)*(x-a)+f(a) for decreasing h to show secant lines tending to the tangent line and connect visual and symbolic derivative definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students choose functions and vary h to see convergence; emphasize geometric interpretation and relation to the limit definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity: Convergence of Fourier series via partial-sum plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use CAS to compute Fourier coefficients and plot partial sums m(N,x) along with the target function k(x)=1-|x| on [-L, L] to study how N affects approximation and where partial sums struggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide Maple (or CAS) templates for coefficient integrals and partial sums; prompt students to explore approximation range, Gibbs phenomena, and convergence issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity: Solving extremal problems in precalculus with technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Model optimization problems (e.g., locating a station along a shoreline to minimize total distance to islands) and use graphing calculators/computers to find minimizing x for D(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to introduce modeling and optimization before students have calculus tools; emphasize model derivation and interpretation of numeric results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity: Using transforms (Fourier) to solve differential equations with CAS
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask participants to solve a differential equation by hand, then use CAS to find the Fourier transform solution and verify by inverse transform and differentiation (example: du/dt - u = e^{-t^2}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CAS commands for transforms and inverse transforms; have students verify solutions symbolically and use CAS as a tool for problems that are tedious by hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity: Investigating convergence of improper integrals numerically and graphically
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Riemann sums, integral commands, and graphing to compare integrals like ∫_1^∞ 1/x^2 and ∫_1^∞ 1/√x, demonstrating differing tail behaviors and convergence properties through numeric approximation and scaled plotting windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students compute partial integrals and use plots on varying windows to visualize tails and compare rates of decay; exploit technology to relate algebraic, numeric, and graphical perspectives.
